name: Nikhil Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for giving me your time, Nikhil. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and this conversation is confidential. What does a typical working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run my own van, a grey Transit Custom on a loan of £280 a month until 2030. In the mornings I do parcel drops for Packwise through their app, then afternoons I do my own direct runs for three local shops, a florist, a hardware store and a bakery. I use AI every day: it plans my route across both jobs, writes my invoices and answers the shop owners while I'm driving.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I still live with my parents to save, which my mum likes and I tolerate. My girlfriend Priya works at a pharmacy, and we want to get engaged next year once I've got the second van. My dad ran a corner shop for 25 years, so business is in the blood, he says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the AI tools are useful, they're just not magic, so use them and get on with it. I'd tell the shop owners the same. Most of the drivers at Packwise would be relieved, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good news, mostly, because my business plan was made for this world. The worry is cash: the van loan eats £280 a month and I've got less than a month's money in the bank. I put everything into the van, so one bad month with the shops and I'm leaning on my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd chase two more local shop contracts this year, maybe the butcher on Market Street and the print shop. I'd use the AI to send them a proper price list and a sample route. And I'd keep Packwise mornings until the shops cover the loan on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Confident, with a knot about the bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad say about your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says don't borrow more than you can pay in a bad month. He learned that the hard way when a supermarket opened near his shop. I listen, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you win the three shops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I walked in with a printed sheet and said I'd do same-day for a flat £8 a run. The florist said yes on the spot because her last driver kept turning up late. The others came from her recommending me.

He thinks most **Packwise drivers** would be relieved.
think: His **business plan** was made for this world, so it's mostly good news.
Cash is the worry: a **£280 van loan** and under a month in the bank.
do: Chase **two more shop contracts**, like the butcher and the print shop.
Use AI to send each one a **price list** and sample route.
Keep **Packwise mornings** until the shops cover the loan.
feel: **Confident**, with a knot about the **bank balance**.

fieldNote: Nikhil is the only driver here running **his own small business**, with three shop contracts.

His father's **corner shop** experience shapes his caution about borrowing.

steps.text: Pitch same-day runs to the butcher and print shop on Market Street
Send each shop an AI-written price list and sample route
Keep Packwise mornings until the shop runs cover the van loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time for anyone who's willing to learn and work. Small businesses can do what big ones do now, with AI as the office. I'd post that on the local business page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me in the short run. AI does my admin, so I can run two vans without hiring an office person. The risk is Packwise, because more drivers will sign up as office jobs go, and the rate will drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a second van on a small loan in the first year and hire someone to drive it, maybe my cousin Arjun. I'd let AI handle bookings and invoices for both vans. And I'd drop Packwise as soon as the shop contracts cover two vans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit nervous about the second loan, but excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A second loan with less than a month saved. What does your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say wait until you've got three months of the loan saved first. He's probably right. Maybe I'd wait six months and save harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever take on someone who's lost an office job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if they're reliable. A good attitude matters more than experience. A laid-off bank clerk who turns up on time beats a delivery driver who doesn't.

Small businesses can now use **AI as the office**, he'd post locally.

**Packwise rates** will drop as laid-off office workers sign up.

Let **AI handle bookings** and invoices for both vans.
**Drop Packwise** once shop contracts cover two vans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the market, and people have to adapt, not cry. But privately, I'd also say small businesses need a fair go against the giants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me. AGI in 2028 helps my admin even more. By 2031 the big firms will have robot vans and charge the shops half what I do, and my van loan runs until 2030. I'd barely have paid it off before the van's worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not buy the second van, full stop. I'd try to sell my van early in 2029, while it's still worth something, and pay off the loan. Then I'd look at running a small robot van franchise if one comes along, or managing deliveries for a local shop chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. My plan was good, and the floor moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people shouldn't cry, but you're scared. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. I'd say adapt in public and lie awake in private. I don't think that makes me a hypocrite, I think it makes me normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya about getting engaged?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I want to wait until I know what I'm doing next. She'd say she doesn't care about the van. My mum would say get married anyway, God provides.

say: This is **the market**, and people should adapt, not cry.
Small businesses need **a fair go** against the giants.
think: By **2031**, big firms with robot vans could charge shops half his price.
His van loan runs until **2030**, so the van could be worthless as he pays it off.
do: **Cancel** plans for a second van entirely.

feel: **Shaken**, because a good plan suddenly feels shaky.
S2.quote: By 2031 the big firms will have robot vans and charge the shops half what I do, and my van loan runs until 2030.
fieldNote: Nikhil's **business plan** depends on years he doesn't get in this picture.
He openly admits **saying one thing** in public and feeling another.
He'd delay **engagement** to Priya, against his mother's view.

steps.text: Shelve plans for the second van
Sell the Transit in early 2029 and clear the loan

Delay getting engaged to Priya until the next job is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to build something, if you're smart about it. I'd say it at the temple to the younger lads too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years to AGI and eight to robots means my van loan is done by 2030 and I'd have four years of profit after. By 2034, I'd want to own a small robot van myself, or run deliveries for several shops with machines. It's tight, but it's a real plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the second van in year two, not year one, and save harder first. I'd use the AI to find more shops and price jobs. I'd get engaged to Priya next year as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Focused. Nervous, but in a useful way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robot vans are too expensive for a small firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big delivery firms grew from small ones, so if robot vans are too expensive I'd lease one or join with two other couriers. I'd find the way, or I'd change course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger lads at the temple?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the AI tools now and get a trade or a skill they can sell. Don't wait for a job to come to you. And don't take a loan you can't pay in a bad month, like my dad says.

say: Five years is enough to **build something**, if you're smart.
He'd tell **younger lads** at the temple the same.
think: His **van loan** ends in 2030, leaving four years of profit.
By **2034** he wants to own a robot van or run machine deliveries.
do: Buy the **second van** in year two after saving harder.
Use **AI to find** more shops and price jobs.
Get **engaged to Priya** next year as planned.
S3.quote: Big delivery firms grew from small ones, so if robot vans are too expensive I'd lease one or join with two other couriers.
fieldNote: Five years lets Nikhil **pay off the van** and still pivot before robots.
He'd consider **joining other couriers** rather than lose to big firms.
His advice to young men repeats his **father's rule** on loans.

steps.text: Buy a second van in year two after saving harder
Use AI to find new shop clients and price runs
Get engaged to Priya next year as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift to anyone with ambition. Use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years to AGI and thirteen to robots means I could build a proper courier firm by 2036 and buy robot vans around 2039. I'd be the one with the machines, not competing with them. It's what my dad would have done if he'd had the chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow to two vans in the first year and three by 2030, with AI doing all the office side. I'd get engaged next year and married the year after. I'd start putting £150 a month into an emergency fund, because my dad's right about bad months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this one that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'll get comfortable. Ten years is long, and comfortable businesses get eaten, like my dad's corner shop before the supermarket came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the drivers you'd hire, when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to train them to run the robot vans, or help them move on. I'm not a charity, but I'd look after my people. That's how my dad treated his Saturday boy.

say: Ten years is **a gift** to anyone with ambition.
People should **use the decade** to build something, he'd say.
think: He could build a **proper courier firm** by 2036.
Around **2039** he'd buy robot vans and own the machines himself.
do: Grow to **two vans** in year one and three by 2030.
Get **engaged next year** and married the year after.
Put **£150 a month** into an emergency fund.
S4.quote: Ten years is long, and comfortable businesses get eaten, like my dad's corner shop before the supermarket came.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Nikhil plan to **own robot vans**, not fight them.
His main worry is **getting comfortable**, drawn from his father's corner shop.
He'd **retrain his drivers** for robot vans, mixing business sense and loyalty.

steps.text: Grow to two vans this year and three by 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robot vans would come before my loan is paid and I'd be undercut by the big firms. What would help is fair access to robot vans for small firms, like leasing schemes, and rules that stop giants from pricing us out. Not handouts, a fair fight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who'll own the robots. If only the big firms own the robots, towns lose their small businesses. If people like me can own one or two, then the money stays on Market Street.

headlineQuote: If only the big firms own the robots, towns lose their small businesses. If people like me can own one or two, then the money stays on Market Street.
portrait: Nikhil is **27**, runs his own van with a loan until 2030 and lives with his parents to save.
He uses **AI daily** for routes, invoices and shop messages, and works for Packwise and three local shops.
He's **traditional and pro-business**, guided by his father's corner shop lessons on borrowing.
Fast AGI **alarms** him because robot vans arrive before his loan is paid; with ten years he's calm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because big firms' robot vans would undercut him before his loan ends.
whatWouldHelp: **Leasing schemes** for small firms to get robot vans, and rules against **giant firms** pricing them out.
